title: The Hart–Fuller debate
subtitle: Law and morality, tested against the grudge informer
objectives: State the terms of the Hart–Fuller debate precisely: whether law and morality are conceptually separate, as Hart's separation thesis maintains, or necessarily connected through law's own internal procedural morality, as Fuller argues
Explain Fuller's eight desiderata of legality and Hart's separation-thesis response with equal precision, including each theorist's own proposed solution to the grudge informer problem
State Radbruch's formula as a third position distinct from both, and apply all three approaches to a single hard case

leadingAuthorities.citation: Hart, 'Positivism and the Separation of Law and Morals' (1958) 71 Harvard Law Review 593
leadingAuthorities.role: Defends the separation thesis against the grudge informer problem; proposes frank retrospective legislation as the honest solution

leadingAuthorities.citation: Fuller, 'Positivism and Fidelity to Law — A Reply to Professor Hart' (1958) 71 Harvard Law Review 630
leadingAuthorities.role: Direct reply to Hart, arguing Nazi enactments failed the internal morality of law so severely that calling them 'law' at all is already a stretch
Develops the eight desiderata — the 'inner morality of law' — in full
The formula naming when extreme injustice defeats a statute's claim to validity — the third position this lesson tests against the other two

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: This is the most examined single debate in the whole module, precisely because it has no settled winner — examiners are testing whether you can argue Hart's case and Fuller's case with equal force, not whether you've picked a side. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of understanding, this brief note appears: 'You can name both theorists — this lesson checks whether you can argue each position as its strongest advocate would.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on stating each position before. The test pool below leans towards scenarios: expect 'which theorist's solution does this represent' rather than 'define the inner morality of law'.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and get the grudge informer facts solid before anything else — every later part in this lesson tests your grip on that one case from a different angle.

overview.hook: In 1944, a German woman denounced her husband to the Nazi authorities for criticising Hitler in private conversation, relying on a wartime statute that made such remarks a capital offence. He was sentenced to death, though in the end sent to the front instead of executed. After the war, a West German court convicted her of unlawfully depriving him of his liberty — which meant deciding, as a matter of law, what to do with the statute she had relied on. Was it law, full stop, however wicked? Or had the Nazi regime's contempt for the basic decencies of legality already disqualified its enactments from being law at all? Two of the twentieth century's most important legal philosophers answered that question directly against each other, in print, in 1958 — and the exchange is still the sharpest way into the entire law-and-morality question.
overview.lawStatedNotice: This lesson teaches a fixed historical debate (1958–1964) and its settled place in the scholarship. There is no legislative development to track; law stated as at 23 September 2026 reflects only that this content remains current teaching.

parts.heading: The grudge informer: the case both sides had to answer
parts.voice: case-narrative — lays out the shared problem before either theorist's answer
body: Strip the case to its bones. A wife wants her husband out of the way. She reports his critical remarks about the Nazi regime to the authorities, citing statutes then in force that criminalised exactly that speech. He is convicted and sentenced to death, though the sentence is commuted to military service. After the war, a West German court is asked to convict her of the crime of illegally depriving her husband of his liberty — and her defence is that, at the time, what she did was entirely lawful under the statute in force.

The court had to decide, as a legal question and not just a moral one, what force that 1934 statute still had. If the statute was valid law at the time, her conduct wasn't unlawful when she did it, and punishing her now looks like retrospective criminalisation of something that was legal. If the statute wasn't really law — because it was too wicked to count as law at all — then her defence collapses and she can be convicted on ordinary principles.

Both Hart and Fuller agreed the wife's conduct deserved condemnation. What divided them was entirely a question about the concept of law itself: does calling something 'law' say anything at all about its moral content, or does a legal system have to clear a moral-procedural bar before the label applies?

components.definition: The post-war German case of a wife prosecuted for denouncing her husband under a Nazi-era statute; it forced courts, and then Hart and Fuller, to decide whether an iniquitous statute that was formally enacted and enforced should be treated as having been valid law at the time.

interaction.prompt: What did Hart and Fuller actually disagree about in the grudge informer case?
options: Whether the wife's conduct was morally wrong — they agreed it was, and disagreed instead about whether the Nazi-era statute she relied on counted as valid law
Whether the wife should be punished at all — Fuller thought she should go free and Hart thought she should be convicted
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — this is the detail students most often miss. Both theorists condemned the wife's conduct and thought some form of punishment was justified; the entire dispute was conceptual, about whether the Nazi statute counted as law.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — both theorists agreed the wife acted wrongly and that she should face some consequence. Their disagreement was purely conceptual: whether the Nazi-era statute she relied on was, as a matter of legal theory, valid law at the time.

parts.heading: Hart's answer: keep the question honest
parts.voice: statute-first — builds from Hart's own words
body: Hart's 1958 article restates the separation thesis from Lesson 5 and applies it directly: the wickedness of a rule, however extreme, is not itself evidence that the rule wasn't law. To say otherwise, Hart argues, blurs together two questions that need to stay separate for clear moral and legal thinking: was this law, and was this law that people had good reason to disobey and that we now have good reason to punish reliance on.

Hart thought the German courts' actual solution — declaring the Nazi statute invalid because it offended natural justice — bought a comfortable outcome at the price of intellectual honesty, and worried about where that kind of reasoning leads. If courts can simply declare a validly enacted statute to have never been law whenever it turns out to be wicked enough, the concept of legal validity stops doing any real work, and 'law' quietly becomes 'law I approve of'.

His own proposed solution is sharper, and worth learning precisely: treat the Nazi statute as having been law at the time — so the wife did nothing unlawful under it then — and, if her conduct still deserves punishment now, enact frankly retrospective legislation saying so openly. That, Hart argues, forces society to confront honestly what it is doing (deliberately punishing an act that was lawful when done, for good moral reasons) rather than disguising a retrospective moral judgment as if it had always been the law.

components.citation: Hart, 'Positivism and the Separation of Law and Morals' (1958) 71 Harv L Rev 593, 619
components.text: If with the Utilitarians we speak plainly, we say that laws may be law but too evil to be obeyed. This is a moral condemnation which everyone can understand and it makes an immediate and obvious claim to moral attention. If, on the other hand, we formulate our objection as an assertion that these evil things are not law, this is a statement which many people do not believe, and if they are disposed to consider it at all, they consider it as an issue of an abstruse and highly general nature to which their attention has, in fact, never earlier been drawn.
elements: Calling a wicked rule 'law, but too evil to obey' keeps the moral objection sharp and immediately understandable
Calling it 'not law at all' turns a clear moral judgment into an abstract conceptual dispute that obscures the real issue
Hart's preferred remedy for the grudge informer case is honest, frankly retrospective legislation, not a backdated denial of validity

interaction.prompt: According to the Hart extract above, what is his central objection to declaring the Nazi statute 'not law at all'?
options: It converts a sharp, immediately understandable moral objection ('law but too evil to obey') into an abstract conceptual dispute that obscures rather than sharpens the moral question
It would let the wife escape all punishment entirely
It contradicts the wording of the Nazi statute itself

parts.heading: Fuller's reply: law has its own inner morality
parts.voice: argumentative — states Fuller's case with full force before any Hart-side rebuttal appears
body: Fuller's reply, published the same year in the same journal, does not appeal to any 'higher law' of substantive natural justice in the way classical natural law does. His claim is narrower, more original, and — on his own account — still recognisably a form of natural law: legality itself has an internal, procedural morality, a set of qualities a system of rules must possess to function as law at all, independent of whether its substantive content is good or bad.

Fuller calls these the eight desiderata of legality, or the 'inner morality of law', and argues the Nazi regime failed several of them so severely and so routinely — secret decrees, retroactive statutes validating past atrocities after the fact, contradictory and constantly shifting directives, a yawning gap between the law on paper and what officials actually did — that whole stretches of Nazi governance were barely a functioning legal system in the first place. If that's right, Fuller argues, there's no need to invoke morality from outside law to defeat the wife's defence: you can say the 1934 statute, as applied within a system that had abandoned legality's own internal standards, was never robustly law to begin with, on grounds internal to what law is.

This is Fuller's most important move against Hart, and the one students most often flatten: he is not smuggling substantive moral content back into the definition of law. He is arguing that procedural fidelity to law's own inner morality is itself already a moral achievement — and that a sufficiently lawless 'legal' system forfeits its claim to the name on its own procedural terms, not because a judge substituted their own view of justice for the statute's content.

components.label: Fuller's eight desiderata (The Morality of Law, 1964)
points: Generality — rules, not ad hoc orders to named individuals
Promulgation — rules must be published and knowable
Non-retroactivity — rules should operate prospectively, not punish past conduct that was lawful when done
Clarity — rules must be intelligible to those bound by them
Non-contradiction — rules must not conflict with each other
Possibility of compliance — rules must not demand the impossible
Constancy through time — rules should not change so often that conduct can never be planned
Congruence — official action must actually match the rules as announced

interaction.prompt: In the passage below, adapted from Fuller's reply to Hart, highlight the sentence that most precisely states his central claim about the Nazi legal system.
interaction.passage: When a system calling itself law is predicated upon a general disregard by judges of the terms of the laws they purport to apply, when this system habitually cures its legal irregularities, not by resort to a rule of law but by retroactive statutes, when it has only to resort to the expedient of forbidding what it can no longer prevent, we begin to wonder whether the acts of a government of this kind can be said to fall within a category that could be called law at all.
interaction.ratioSentence: we begin to wonder whether the acts of a government of this kind can be said to fall within a category that could be called law at all

parts.heading: Two solutions, head to head
parts.voice: structural — juxtaposes both theorists' actual proposed answers without declaring a winner
body: Lay the two solutions to the grudge informer case side by side, because the difference is more precise than 'Hart says law, Fuller says not law' — each theorist reaches their conclusion by a genuinely different route, and each pays a genuine cost for it.

Hart's route: the Nazi statute was valid law at the time (this preserves a clean, general separation between legal validity and moral merit). The wife committed no legal wrong under it then. If she deserves punishment now, that requires society to pass an honest, openly retrospective law saying so — a cost Hart accepts because he thinks the alternative (disguised retroactivity dressed up as 'it was never law') is worse for the rule of law in the long run.

Fuller's route: the wider Nazi system of secret, retroactive, self-contradicting decrees had degraded so far from the eight desiderata that describing it as a functioning legal system misdescribes what was actually happening — so the 1934 statute, embedded in that system, never had a strong claim to be law on its own procedural terms. This lets a court convict the wife without any frankly retrospective legislation — but at the cost of making 'is this law?' turn on a court's own assessment of how badly a regime failed on generality, clarity, congruence and the rest, a judgment call Hart worried was exactly as unstable as the 'higher law' approach he was trying to avoid.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often write that 'Fuller thinks the Nazi regime was evil, so its laws weren't law' — collapsing his procedural argument into ordinary substantive natural law.
components.whyItsWrong: Fuller's argument is not that the content of Nazi law was unjust, though he certainly thought it was — it is that the way the Nazi system operated (secrecy, retroactivity, contradiction, non-congruence between announced rules and official conduct) failed law's own internal, procedural standards so badly that it barely functioned as a rule-following system at all. A regime could, in principle, pursue substantively wicked goals while scrupulously observing Fuller's eight desiderata — Fuller's test would then have far less to say against it, which is precisely why critics argue his theory is a thinner form of natural law than it first appears.

interaction.prompt: Which of these two proposed judicial approaches to the grudge informer case is Hart's, rather than Fuller's?
interaction.scenarioA: The court treats the 1934 statute as having been valid law at the time (so the wife committed no offence under it then), and any punishment of her now would require Parliament to pass an openly retrospective statute saying so.
interaction.scenarioB: The court holds that the wider system of secret decrees, retroactive validations and official conduct that ignored announced rules meant the Nazi 'legal system' had already forfeited its claim to be a functioning legal order, so the 1934 statute carried little weight as law.
interaction.explanation: A is Hart's route: preserve the separation thesis by treating the statute as having been valid law, and solve the grudge informer problem with honest, openly retrospective legislation rather than a backdated denial of validity. B is Fuller's route, grounded in the collapse of the inner morality of law across the wider system.

parts.heading: Radbruch's formula: a third position
parts.voice: reflective — introduces the position that predates, and partly frames, the whole debate
body: Before Hart and Fuller argued in print, the German legal philosopher Gustav Radbruch — writing in 1946, having lived through the collapse of the Weimar Republic and the Nazi regime himself — had already proposed the solution German courts actually used. Radbruch had been a legal positivist before the war; the experience of Nazi law changed his mind, and his 1946 essay is in part a public recantation.

Radbruch's formula has two parts, and precision matters here: ordinarily, positive law takes priority over ideas of justice even when its content is unjust or inexpedient, because legal certainty is itself a value worth protecting — this is the 'intolerability formula'. But where the conflict between a statute and justice reaches an intolerable degree, the statute must yield to justice as 'flawed law'. A second, narrower 'disqualifying formula' goes further still: where a law does not even attempt to strive for justice — where it deliberately denies the equality of human beings, as in laws targeting a group for extermination — it is not just flawed, it altogether lacks the very nature of law.

Notice how Radbruch's formula differs from both Hart and Fuller. Unlike Hart, he holds that extreme injustice can strip a statute of legal validity outright. Unlike Fuller, his test is explicitly substantive — the intolerable degree of injustice in the rule's content — not a procedural failure of generality, clarity or congruence. Radbruch's is the position that comes closest to classical natural law's lex injusta non est lex, but narrowed deliberately to extreme cases, precisely so that ordinary unjust laws remain law and only the most intolerable ones are disqualified.

components.definition: The position that positive law ordinarily takes priority over justice even when unjust, unless the conflict between statute and justice reaches such an intolerable degree that the statute must yield as 'flawed law' — with a narrower 'disqualifying formula' for laws that deliberately deny human equality altogether.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that Radbruch's formula treats every unjust law as automatically invalid?
sliderLabels: Confident — every unjust law loses validity
Confident — only intolerably or extremely unjust law loses validity
interaction.correctPosition: Confident — only intolerably or extremely unjust law loses validity
interaction.explanation: Radbruch is explicit that legal certainty ordinarily wins even against unjust content — the ordinary rule is that positive law takes priority. Only where the injustice reaches an intolerable degree does the statute yield as 'flawed law', and only where a law denies human equality outright does it lose the nature of law entirely. This deliberate narrowness is what distinguishes his formula from a sweeping natural law claim that any unjust rule simply isn't law.

testPool.prompt: State, in one sentence, what Hart and Fuller actually disagreed about.
acceptableAnswers: whether an extremely unjust statute can still be valid law
whether law and morality are conceptually separate or necessarily connected through law's inner morality
testPool.modelAnswer: They disagreed over whether calling something 'law' is a purely descriptive, morally neutral question (Hart's separation thesis) or whether law necessarily has to satisfy an internal procedural morality to count as law at all (Fuller's inner morality of law) — tested directly against the grudge informer case.

testPool.prompt: Name Fuller's eight desiderata of legality.
acceptableAnswers: generality, promulgation, non-retroactivity, clarity, non-contradiction, possibility of compliance, constancy, congruence
testPool.modelAnswer: Generality, promulgation, non-retroactivity, clarity, non-contradiction, possibility of compliance, constancy through time, and congruence between announced rules and official action.

testPool.prompt: What solution did Hart propose for punishing the grudge informer, consistent with the separation thesis?
options: Enact frankly retrospective legislation, openly punishing conduct that was lawful when done
Declare that the Nazi statute had secretly never been valid law all along

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of Fuller's eight desiderata of legality?
options: Promulgation
Non-retroactivity
Substantive fairness of the rule's content
Congruence between announced rules and official action
testPool.trapExplanation: This is the trap the whole lesson is built to catch: Fuller's desiderata are procedural, about how a system of rules is made and administered, not about whether the content of any given rule is substantively fair. Adding 'substantive fairness' as a desideratum would turn Fuller into a classical natural lawyer, which he explicitly denied being.

testPool.prompt: A student writes: 'Fuller and Radbruch are really saying the same thing — that sufficiently unjust law stops being law.' What is the strongest response to this claim?
options: The student is correct without qualification

The two tests are genuinely different: Radbruch's test asks whether the rule's substantive content reaches an intolerable degree of injustice, while Fuller's test asks whether the system's procedures (generality, promulgation, non-retroactivity and the rest) have collapsed — a regime could satisfy one test and fail the other
Radbruch and Fuller never addressed the same historical episode, so no comparison is possible
testPool.trapExplanation: The two positions look similar because they reach a similar conclusion about Nazi law, but the reasoning is different in kind — Radbruch's formula is explicitly substantive (about how unjust the rule's content is), while Fuller insists his test is procedural (about how the system of rules is made and administered). Conflating them erases exactly the distinction that makes Fuller's position original.

testPool.prompt: Radbruch's formula states that positive law 'takes precedence even when its content is unjust...unless the conflict between statute and justice reaches such an intolerable degree that the statute...must yield to justice.' What does the phrase 'intolerable degree' signal about how the formula is meant to operate?
options: It is meant to apply only to extreme cases, leaving ordinary unjust laws valid — a deliberately narrow exception, not a general licence to override statutes with judicial views of justice
It means any statute a judge personally dislikes can be disregarded
It has no legal significance and is merely rhetorical flourish

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that illustrates a breach of Fuller's 'congruence' desideratum specifically.
testPool.scenarioText: A regime publishes a criminal code stating clearly that only conduct occurring after enactment can be punished. In practice, however, officials routinely detain and punish people for conduct that took place years before the code existed, ignoring the published rule entirely.
tappableSpans: publishes a criminal code stating clearly
only conduct occurring after enactment can be punished
officials routinely detain and punish people for conduct that took place years before
testPool.feedbackCorrect: That's congruence failing specifically: the announced rule is clear, general and prospective on its face, but official action systematically departs from it — the gap between the rule as written and the rule as applied is exactly what the congruence desideratum targets.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the gap between the rule as published and what officials actually do, rather than the content of the rule itself. Congruence is breached when official conduct fails to match the announced rules, regardless of how well-drafted those rules look on paper.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that best supports Hart's objection to the German courts' actual approach in the grudge informer case.
testPool.scenarioText: The West German court declared the 1934 statute had never been valid law because it offended natural justice. Commentators later noted that this reasoning gave no clear, general test for identifying which other statutes from the same period should also be treated as never having been law, leaving the boundary to be worked out case by case after the fact.
tappableSpans: declared the 1934 statute had never been valid law
gave no clear, general test for identifying which other statutes
the boundary to be worked out case by case after the fact
testPool.correctSpan: the boundary to be worked out case by case after the fact
testPool.explanation: This is precisely Hart's worry: once courts can declare a validly enacted statute never to have been law whenever it seems wicked enough, the line between law and non-law stops being a stable, general test and becomes an unpredictable, after-the-fact judgment — which is exactly the instability Hart thought his frankly-retrospective-legislation solution avoided.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario would most trouble Fuller's procedural test while leaving Radbruch's substantive test comparatively untroubled?
testPool.scenarioA: A regime enacts, with full generality, promulgation, clarity, prospectivity, and consistent official enforcement exactly as announced, a statute that deliberately strips a named minority of all legal personhood and protection.
testPool.scenarioB: A regime governs through secret, constantly changing, self-contradictory decrees that are never published and are enforced in ways that bear no relation to what was announced, in pursuit of otherwise unremarkable policy goals.
testPool.explanation: A is the harder case for Fuller: the regime satisfies the eight desiderata impeccably (procedurally flawless) while pursuing a substantively monstrous goal, which is exactly the criticism levelled at Fuller's theory — that a system can be procedurally excellent and still gravely unjust. Radbruch's substantive test, by contrast, is well suited to catching A, since it asks directly about the intolerable injustice of the rule's content.

testPool.prompt: A statute is clear, published, prospective, consistent, and consistently enforced exactly as written — but its content mandates the confiscation of a targeted group's property purely on grounds of their ethnicity. Applying Radbruch's disqualifying formula specifically, what result follows?
options: The statute may lack the very nature of law altogether, since it deliberately denies the equality of human beings rather than merely being flawed or unjust in degree
The statute is automatically valid because it satisfies every one of Fuller's procedural desiderata
Radbruch's formula has nothing to say about property law, only criminal law
testPool.explanation: This is the disqualifying formula specifically, distinct from the milder 'intolerability' branch: a law that does not even attempt to strive for justice, by deliberately denying the equality of human beings, is not merely flawed law that yields to justice in extreme cases — Radbruch holds it lacks the nature of law altogether, regardless of how procedurally impeccable its enactment was.

testPool.prompt: A post-conflict state's transitional court must decide whether to convict a former official who enforced a now-repudiated regime's clearly published, consistently applied, but severely discriminatory land statute. Using Hart's, Fuller's and Radbruch's approaches in turn, analyse how each would resolve the question of whether that statute was ever valid law.
factsToOrder: The statute was clear, published and consistently enforced as written
Its substantive content was severely discriminatory against a targeted group
Hart's separation thesis asks only about pedigree, not moral content
Fuller's test asks whether the system satisfied the eight procedural desiderata
Radbruch's formula asks whether the statute's injustice reached an intolerable, or disqualifying, degree

modelAnswer.issue: Whether a clearly published, procedurally impeccable but substantively discriminatory statute was ever valid law, under Hart's, Fuller's and Radbruch's respective approaches.
modelAnswer.rule: Hart: validity depends on pedigree (enactment, sanction, recognition), not moral content — the statute was law, however discriminatory, and any post hoc punishment should be by frank retrospective legislation. Fuller: validity depends on the system's fidelity to the eight procedural desiderata, irrespective of substantive content. Radbruch: ordinarily positive law prevails even when unjust, unless the injustice reaches an intolerable degree, or the law denies human equality outright, in which case it is disqualified as law.
modelAnswer.application: On Hart's approach, the statute was valid law at the time because it was properly enacted, clear and enforced — the official's conduct in applying it was lawful then, and any conviction now requires openly retrospective legislation. On Fuller's approach, this is the hard case for his theory: because the statute was clear, published, prospective and congruently enforced, it satisfies the eight desiderata despite its discriminatory content, so Fuller's own test gives little traction for denying it was law — a limitation critics press hardest here. On Radbruch's approach, severe discrimination against a targeted group is precisely the kind of substantive injustice his formula is built to catch — if the discrimination reaches an intolerable degree, or amounts to a denial of the group's basic legal equality, the statute is either flawed law that must yield, or is disqualified from being law at all.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The three approaches diverge sharply on this fact pattern precisely because it is procedurally clean but substantively unjust: Hart and Fuller both struggle to deny the statute's validity on their own terms, while Radbruch's substantive test is the one most capable of stripping it of legal status — illustrating why no single theory resolves every hard case in this debate.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that Hart's position in this debate amounts to saying the Nazi regime's statutes should have been obeyed?
sliderLabels: Confident — that's what Hart is saying
Confident — Hart never says the statutes should have been obeyed
testPool.correctPosition: Confident — Hart never says the statutes should have been obeyed
testPool.explanation: This is the most common misreading of Hart in this debate. His claim is only that the statutes were valid law — a question of pedigree — not that they were law people had good moral reason to obey. Hart is explicit that a law can be law and still be so evil that it must be resisted or disobeyed; the separation thesis keeps those two judgments distinct, it does not collapse validity into an obligation to comply.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating Fuller's inner morality of law as a substantive test in disguise — as if he were simply saying 'unjust law isn't law'. He isn't: his eight desiderata are procedural, about how a system of rules is made and administered, which is exactly why a procedurally impeccable but substantively unjust statute is the hardest case for his theory, and exactly where Radbruch's explicitly substantive formula does different work.
